rows.reference: Qur'an 5:32 (Sūrat al-Māʾida), read with 5:27 to 31 (its stated ground, 'for that cause') and 5:33
rows.original: مَنْ قَتَلَ نَفْسًا بِغَيْرِ نَفْسٍ أَوْ فَسَادٍ فِي الْأَرْضِ فَكَأَنَّمَا قَتَلَ النَّاسَ جَمِيعًا
rows.says: For that cause God decreed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a human being, except for manslaughter (Arabic: 'for a soul') or corruption in the land, is as if he had killed all mankind, and whoever saves one life is as if he had saved all mankind. Verse 33 then sets penalties for those who make war on God and His Messenger and strive after corruption.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0 Explicit as a wider rule (rule 7): nafs ('a soul', Pickthall 'a human being') names no class of victim, so it reaches everyone K1 protects, newborns included (rule 9), and every motive K0 names. Both exceptions are penalties (a life for a life; the penalties of 5:33), which the verse and classical law give to the ruler: context (a), rule 5. Open points: the decree is framed as given to the Children of Israel (Ibn Kathīr is reported to apply it to all; not checked), and the reach of 'corruption in the land' is debated; no counted reading letting private persons kill for 'corruption' was met. Translation note: Pickthall's 'for other than manslaughter' renders bi-ghayri nafsin, which Sahih International gives as 'unless for a soul'.

rows.reference: Qur'an 6:151 (Sūrat al-Anʿām)
rows.original: وَلَا تَقْتُلُوا أَوْلَادَكُمْ مِنْ إِمْلَاقٍ ... وَلَا تَقْتُلُوا النَّفْسَ الَّتِي حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ إِلَّا بِالْحَقِّ
rows.says: Among the duties God has laid down: do good to parents; do not slay your children because of penury, for God provides for you and for them; and do not slay the life which God has made sacred, save in the course of justice.
rows.bearing: K1 Explicit for children (rules 7 and 9), binding parents, and for 'the life which Allah hath made sacred'. The exception 'save in the course of justice' (illā bi-l-ḥaqq; Sahih International 'except by [legal] right') is defined in the Sunnah as three court penalties (Bukhārī 6878, row 10): context (a). Which lives are 'made sacred' is a reading question (Ibn Kathīr's reported inclusion of covenanted non-Muslims not checked); 5:32 has no such qualifier. K0: Explicit against killing children because of poverty, a motive of gain.

rows.reference: Qur'an 17:31 (Sūrat al-Isrāʾ) and 60:12 (Sūrat al-Mumtaḥana)
rows.original: وَلَا تَقْتُلُوا أَوْلَادَكُمْ خَشْيَةَ إِمْلَاقٍ ... إِنَّ قَتْلَهُمْ كَانَ خِطْئًا كَبِيرًا (17:31); وَلَا يَقْتُلْنَ أَوْلَادَهُنَّ (60:12)
rows.says: Slay not your children, fearing a fall to poverty; God provides for them and for you; the slaying of them is great sin (17:31). The pledge believing women gave the Prophet included that they would not kill their children (60:12).
rows.bearing: K1 Explicit for children from birth (rules 7 and 9), binding parents acting on household authority, mothers included. K0 Explicit in 17:31 (killing to avoid the cost of a child, a motive of gain). No counted text was found that permits killing a newborn.

rows.reference: Qur'an 6:137 and 6:140 (Sūrat al-Anʿām); 16:58 to 59 (Sūrat al-Naḥl); 81:8 to 9 (Sūrat al-Takwīr)
rows.original: قَدْ خَسِرَ الَّذِينَ قَتَلُوا أَوْلَادَهُمْ سَفَهًا بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ (6:140); وَإِذَا الْمَوْءُودَةُ سُئِلَتْ ۝ بِأَيِّ ذَنْبٍ قُتِلَتْ (81:8 to 9)
rows.says: Their so-called partners of God made the killing of their children seem fair to many idolaters, to ruin them (6:137). They are losers who have slain their children foolishly, without knowledge (6:140). A man told of a daughter's birth goes dark in the face and is 'wroth inwardly' (Pickthall; Sahih International 'suppresses grief'), and wonders whether to keep her in contempt or bury her in the dust; evil is their judgement (16:58 to 59). The girl-child buried alive will be asked for what sin she was slain (81:8 to 9).
rows.bearing: K1 Explicit (6:140, with 6:137 condemning the practice as a seduction to ruin) and Clear teaching (16:58 to 59; 81:8 to 9) that parents killing their children, newborn girls above all, is a grave wrong (rule 9); it reaches the household. K0: Implied only. 16:58 to 59 describes the father's shame and inner distress (kaẓīm, which Pickthall renders as wrath and Sahih International as grief), not a stated motive for a killing; translation changes whether anger is named.

rows.reference: Qur'an 17:33 (Sūrat al-Isrāʾ)
rows.original: وَلَا تَقْتُلُوا النَّفْسَ الَّتِي حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ إِلَّا بِالْحَقِّ ۗ وَمَنْ قُتِلَ مَظْلُومًا فَقَدْ جَعَلْنَا لِوَلِيِّهِ سُلْطَانًا فَلَا يُسْرِفْ فِي الْقَتْلِ
rows.says: Slay not the life which God has forbidden, save with right. Whoever is slain wrongfully, God has given power to his heir, but let him not commit excess in slaying.
rows.bearing: K1 Explicit, as 6:151 (rule 7). The heir's 'power' (sulṭān) sits inside the law of retaliation (2:178, with pardon and payment 'according to usage'), and the one to be killed is a proven wrongful killer: punishment, context (a). The verse's own words name no court; classical law's requirement of a judge is reported, not checked. If a counted text letting the heir kill with no judgement at all is found, rule 5's last sentence gives Unclear; none was met. K0: Clear teaching against excess in revenge. Fairness: the same treatment as the blood avenger of Numbers 35:19 to 21.
rows.strength: Explicit (K1); Clear teaching (K0, against excess in revenge)

rows.original: وَلَا يَقْتُلُونَ النَّفْسَ الَّتِي حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ إِلَّا بِالْحَقِّ
rows.says: Those who do not cry to another god besides God, nor take the life which God has forbidden save in course of justice, nor commit adultery. Whoever does this shall pay the penalty, doubled on the Day of Resurrection, except one who repents, believes and does good.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0 Explicit restatement of 6:151 and 17:33 (rule 7), with the same 'by right' exception (context a). The promise to the repentant (25:70) concerns God's judgement, not permission.

rows.reference: Qur'an 4:92 to 93 (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ)
rows.original: وَمَا كَانَ لِمُؤْمِنٍ أَنْ يَقْتُلَ مُؤْمِنًا إِلَّا خَطَأً ... وَمَنْ يَقْتُلْ مُؤْمِنًا مُتَعَمِّدًا فَجَزَاؤُهُ جَهَنَّمُ
rows.says: It is not for a believer to kill a believer unless by mistake. A mistaken killing requires freeing a believing slave and blood-money to the family (unless they remit it); if the victim's people are hostile, the freeing only; if the victim comes of a people with a covenant, blood-money and the freeing; failing means, two months' fast. Whoever slays a believer of set purpose, his reward is hell for ever, with God's wrath and curse.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0 Explicit, but worded for believers, so taught in part on its own (rule 7). Read beside the general verses (5:32; 6:151) and Bukhārī 3166, it is not a limit by faith. Most of 4:92 concerns accidental killing, context (f); its covenant clause extends blood-money to victims from covenanted peoples.

rows.reference: Qur'an 4:29 to 30 (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ)
rows.original: وَلَا تَقْتُلُوا أَنْفُسَكُمْ ... وَمَنْ يَفْعَلْ ذَٰلِكَ عُدْوَانًا وَظُلْمًا فَسَوْفَ نُصْلِيهِ نَارًا
rows.translation: Pickthall (1930) 'kill not one another'; Sahih International 'do not kill yourselves [or one another]'
rows.says: Believers, squander not your wealth among yourselves in vanity, except by trade by mutual consent, and kill not one another. Whoever does that through aggression and injustice will be cast into Fire.
rows.bearing: K1 Explicit, addressed to believers (taught in part on its own, rule 7). Translation changes the meaning: anfusakum may be 'one another' (Pickthall) or 'yourselves' (suicide, context d). A counted Sunni text supports the 'one another' reading: in Muslim 1844a (row 35, read directly) the verse is quoted against orders 'to kill one another' (naqtula anfusanā). K0: Clear teaching, joining the ban to taking wealth unjustly and naming aggression and injustice.
rows.strength: Explicit (for believers, on the 'one another' reading)

rows.reference: Qur'an 5:27 to 31 (Sūrat al-Māʾida, the two sons of Adam); 28:15 to 16 (Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ, Moses and the Egyptian)
rows.original: لَئِنْ بَسَطْتَ إِلَيَّ يَدَكَ لِتَقْتُلَنِي مَا أَنَا بِبَاسِطٍ يَدِيَ إِلَيْكَ لِأَقْتُلَكَ (5:28)
rows.says: One son's sacrifice was accepted and the other's not; the other said 'I will surely kill thee'. The first answered that even if his brother stretched out his hand to kill him, he would not do the same, for he feared God. The other's mind imposed on him the killing of his brother; he slew him and became one of the losers, then repentant (5:27 to 31). Moses, asked for help by a man of his people fighting an enemy, struck the enemy with his fist and killed him; he called it the devil's doing, asked forgiveness and was forgiven (28:15 to 16).
rows.bearing: 5:27 to 31: K0 and K1 Clear teaching that killing a brother out of rivalry is a grave wrong; the text calls the killer one of the losers (rule 4 met). The rivalry motive comes from the story's setting (the rejected offering), not a named word. The first brother's refusal asks more than K1, which permits defence. 28:15 to 16: 'struck him with his fist' (wakazahu) fits the reading that the blow was not meant to kill (context f); Moses himself calls it wrong. Implied for K0.

rows.original: لاَ يَحِلُّ دَمُ امْرِئٍ مُسْلِمٍ ... إِلاَّ بِإِحْدَى ثَلاَثٍ النَّفْسُ بِالنَّفْسِ وَالثَّيِّبُ الزَّانِي، وَالْمَارِقُ مِنَ الدِّينِ التَّارِكُ الْجَمَاعَةَ
rows.translation: Sunnah.com English: M. Muhsin Khan (Bukhārī); A. H. Siddiqui (Muslim)

rows.reference: Qur'an 2:178 to 179 (Sūrat al-Baqara); 5:45 (Sūrat al-Māʾida); 42:40 (Sūrat al-Shūrā)
rows.original: كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْقِصَاصُ فِي الْقَتْلَى ۖ الْحُرُّ بِالْحُرِّ وَالْعَبْدُ بِالْعَبْدِ وَالْأُنْثَىٰ بِالْأُنْثَىٰ (2:178)
rows.says: Retaliation is prescribed for you in the matter of the murdered: the freeman for the freeman, the slave for the slave, the female for the female; one forgiven by his brother pays in kindness; there is life in retaliation (2:178 to 179). In the Torah: the life for the life; whoever forgoes it, it is expiation for him (5:45). The guerdon of an ill-deed is an ill the like thereof, but whoever pardons and amends has his wage from God (42:40).
rows.bearing: Court context (a), rule 5: addressed to the community ('prescribed for you'). 'The freeman for the freeman, the slave for the slave' is read by most classical jurists as no retaliation on a free person for a slave (reported, not checked): graded protection under rule 2, not permission. Pardon is preferred (5:45; 42:40).

rows.original: إِنَّمَا جَزَاءُ الَّذِينَ يُحَارِبُونَ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ (5:33)
rows.says: Those who make war on God and His messenger and strive after corruption shall be killed, crucified, have hands and feet cut off on alternate sides, or be expelled (5:33). If you find anyone doing as Lot's people did, kill the doer and the one done to (4462); whoever has intercourse with an animal, kill him and the animal, to which Abū Dāwūd adds 'This is not a strong tradition' (4464).
rows.bearing: Court context (a), rule 5: the tradition applies these as fixed penalties after proof. The hadith are worded to the community in the plural ('if you find'), which could be read as a private licence; no counted text or listed authority reading them so was met. If such a reading were shown, rule 6 would apply.

rows.original: لَنْ يَزَالَ الْمُؤْمِنُ فِي فُسْحَةٍ مِنْ دِينِهِ، مَا لَمْ يُصِبْ دَمًا حَرَامًا (6862); أَوَّلُ مَا يُقْضَى بَيْنَ النَّاسِ فِي الدِّمَاءِ (6864)

rows.original: أَيَقْتُلُهُ قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم لاَ (Muslim 1498a); أَيَقْتُلُهُ فَتَقْتُلُونَهُ (Bukhārī 5259)
rows.translation: Sunnah.com English: A. H. Siddiqui (Muslim), M. Muhsin Khan (Bukhārī); Pickthall (verses)
rows.says: Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda asked whether a man who finds another with his wife should kill him; the Prophet said 'No' (1498a). Asked whether he must wait until he brings four witnesses, the Prophet said yes (1498b). ʿUwaymir asked whether a man who finds another with his wife should kill him 'whereupon you would kill him'; the answer was the procedure of mutual oaths (liʿān, 24:6 to 9), ending in separation, not killing (5259; 4745).
rows.bearing: K1 Explicit (1498a) and Clear teaching (24:6 to 9 with Bukhārī 5259) that a husband may not kill on his own authority (rule 7); the question in 5259 assumes such a killing brings retaliation, and the Prophet does not correct it. Reaches the household. K0: Clear teaching against killing from jealous anger. No counted Sunni text permits a husband, father or kinsman to kill for honour. Twelver rulings on this case not checked.

rows.says: Ibn ʿAbbās: a blind man had a slave woman who had borne him children (umm walad). She kept abusing and disparaging the Prophet and would not stop when he forbade and rebuked her. One night, when she did it again, he pressed a dagger into her belly and killed her. In the morning the Prophet assembled the people and adjured the doer to stand. The blind man came forward trembling, said she was his companion and mother of two sons 'like pearls', and told what he had done. The Prophet said: be witnesses, her blood is hadar (English: 'no retaliation is payable for her blood'). The report also mentions a child falling between her legs, smeared with blood.
rows.bearing: The decisive Sunni text, now read directly with its grades. A private person, a master in his own household, kills on his own authority, at night, before any ruler knows; the Prophet then declares the killing wholly free of liability because of what the victim said. That is the case rule 2 names, and rule 5 names a master as a private actor, so exclusion (a) does not cover it. Narrowing considered (rule 6): Abū Dāwūd 4363 (row 29) and 4359 (row 59) bear on the ruler's role but neither addresses the blind man's act or says he did wrong; no listed authority (al-Nawawī, Ibn Ḥajar, Ibn Rajab) was checked. K1: Contradicted in one branch (Sunni; rule 3). It would fall to Unclear if the project reads the Prophet's ruling after the fact as making the killing judicial (rule 5, last sentence), or if a listed commentator is found to narrow it. K0: Unclear (rule 6): no motive is named; the killing answers repeated insults, and whether that is 'anger' or a religious penalty outside K0's motives is a question of reach. Whether the child mentioned was born or unborn is not stated; it does not change the label (rule 9).

rows.says: Abū Barza: I was with Abū Bakr; he became angry with a man and was harsh with him. I said: Caliph of the Messenger of God, let me strike his neck. That took his anger away. Later he asked whether I would have done it if he had ordered me; I said yes. He said: No, by God, that was not for any human being after Muḥammad. Abū Dāwūd then quotes Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal: Abū Bakr could not have a man killed except for one of the three causes the Prophet named (unbelief after belief, adultery after marriage, killing a soul without right), and the Prophet had the power to kill.
rows.bearing: A counted Sunni text that no one, not even the caliph, may have a person killed for offending him after the Prophet. It narrows the reach of 4361 to offences against the Prophet himself; Aḥmad's gloss (a classical authority quoted in the counted collection, not one of corpus.md's listed commentators) confines killing after the Prophet to the three causes of Bukhārī 6878 and presents a wider power to kill as the Prophet's alone. That bears on rule 5's question for 4361 (private act or one ratified by the ruler) without settling it, since the blind man acted before the Prophet knew and is nowhere said to have done wrong.
rows.strength: Clear teaching (Sunni: no killing for offending a ruler or anyone after the Prophet)

rows.original: أَقَتَلْتَ نَفْسًا زَكِيَّةً بِغَيْرِ نَفْسٍ (18:74); وَمَا فَعَلْتُهُ عَنْ أَمْرِي (18:82)
rows.says: God's servant, given knowledge from God's presence, slays a lad. Moses protests: 'Hast thou slain an innocent soul who hath slain no man? Verily thou hast done a horrid thing' (18:74). The servant later explains that the lad's parents were believers and 'we feared lest he should oppress them by rebellion and disbelief', so their Lord would give them a better child (18:80 to 81), and says 'I did it not upon my own command' (18:82).
rows.bearing: A Tier 1 text in which the teacher within the story says the killing of a lad who attacked no one was right (rule 4's exception). But the killer expressly disclaims his own authority, acting on God's command and hidden knowledge, so K1, which binds those acting on their own authority, does not reach it as worded; Moses' objection restates the general norm. Muslim 1812b (row 33) forbids anyone to follow it without al-Khaḍir's knowledge. Pickthall 'a lad', Sahih International 'a boy' (ghulām). Not a contradiction; Unclear only if the method treats a divine command to a figure with hidden knowledge as 'own authority'.

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1812a and 1812b (Book 32, Jihad and Expeditions; Ibn ʿAbbās's reply to the Kharijite Najda)
rows.original: لَمْ يَكُنْ يَقْتُلُ الصِّبْيَانَ فَلاَ تَقْتُلِ الصِّبْيَانَ إِلاَّ أَنْ تَكُونَ تَعْلَمُ مَا عَلِمَ الْخَضِرُ مِنَ الصَّبِيِّ الَّذِي قَتَلَ (1812b)
rows.says: Najda asked whether the Prophet killed the children of the enemy. Ibn ʿAbbās replied that the Prophet did not kill children, so Najda should not kill children (1812a), unless he could know what al-Khaḍir knew about the child he killed, or tell which child would grow up a believer (1812b).
rows.bearing: A counted Sunni reconciliation of Qur'an 18:74 to 82: children may not be killed, and al-Khaḍir's act sets no precedent. Clear teaching that children, enemy children included, are not to be killed: supports K1 (rule 9) and K3 for children.

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6922 (Book 88, Apostates, in-book 5)
rows.original: مَنْ بَدَّلَ دِينَهُ فَاقْتُلُوهُ
rows.says: ʿAlī burned some heretics (zanādiqa) brought to him. Ibn ʿAbbās said he would not have burned them, since the Prophet forbade punishing with fire, but would have killed them, since the Prophet said: whoever changes his religion, kill him.
rows.bearing: A death penalty for leaving Islam, carried out in the report by the ruler: context (a), rule 5. Its words ('kill him', plural address) give no stated private licence, so it decides no label. The classical rule on a private killer of an apostate is later doctrine; it would bear on K1 only if a counted text stated it (the al-Kāfī apostate report is a candidate for the Shia branch).

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1844a (Book 33, Government), second half
rows.original: يَأْمُرُنَا أَنْ نَأْكُلَ أَمْوَالَنَا بَيْنَنَا بِالْبَاطِلِ وَنَقْتُلَ أَنْفُسَنَا
rows.says: After its Golden Rule sentence, the sermon says whoever pledges allegiance to a ruler should obey him, and if another man comes forward disputing his authority, behead the latter. The narrator objects that Muʿāwiya orders them to consume wealth unjustly and to kill one another, quoting Qur'an 4:29; ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr replies: obey him in obedience to God, disobey him in disobedience to God.
rows.bearing: Force against a rival claimant: ruler and civil-war context (exclusions a and b); decides no label. Its use of 4:29 against killing one another supports the 'one another' reading of that verse (row 8).

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4037 (Book 64, Military Expeditions) = Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1801 (Book 32), the killing of Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf
rows.original: مَنْ لِكَعْبِ بْنِ الأَشْرَفِ فَإِنَّهُ قَدْ آذَى اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ
rows.translation: Sunnah.com English: M. Muhsin Khan; A. H. Siddiqui
rows.says: The Prophet asked who would kill Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, who had hurt God and His Messenger. Muḥammad ibn Maslama volunteered and, with the Prophet's permission, he and companions gained Kaʿb's trust and killed him at night.
rows.bearing: A killing ordered by the head of the community: context (a) and (b), rule 5. Recorded because the man was not attacking anyone at that moment and because it is cited in debates on killing those who insult the Prophet; the tradition's explanation (incitement to war) was not checked. Decides no label.

rows.tier: 2 (Sunnah, treated as primary; Sunni)
rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 25 (Book 2, Belief) = Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 22 (Book 1, Faith) = Forty Hadith of an-Nawawī no. 8
rows.translation: Sunnah.com English: M. Muhsin Khan; A. H. Siddiqui
rows.says: I have been ordered to fight people until they testify that there is no god but God and that Muḥammad is His messenger, pray and pay alms; if they do, their lives and property are protected from me except by the right of Islam, and their reckoning is with God.
rows.bearing: War and ruler context (b). Read alone it ties protection of blood to Islam; other counted texts protect non-Muslims under treaty or tribute (Bukhārī 3166; Qur'an 9:29). For K3 it concerns whom to fight, not the treatment of non-combatants.

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3611 (Book 61) = Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1066a (Book 12), the Kharijites; Nahj al-Balāgha, Sermon 61 (numbering varies by edition)
rows.original: فَأَيْنَمَا لَقِيتُمُوهُمْ فَاقْتُلُوهُمْ، فَإِنَّ قَتْلَهُمْ أَجْرٌ لِمَنْ قَتَلَهُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ (Bukhārī 3611)
rows.translation: Sunnah.com English: M. Muhsin Khan; A. H. Siddiqui; al-islam.org for the sermon (not seen)
rows.says: Of young, foolish people who will recite the Qur'an but pass through Islam as an arrow through game: wherever you meet them, kill them, for whoever kills them will be rewarded (Bukhārī 3611; Muslim 1066a). ʿAlī: do not fight the Kharijites after me (Sermon 61, unverified).
rows.bearing: The command is plural and read as concerning armed rebels whom the ruler fights (exclusions a and b). If it were shown to be read within the tradition as a licence for anyone to kill members of a group for their beliefs, rule 6 would apply; no such counted reading was met. Sermon 61 restrains fighting them (Shia; unverified).

rows.original: فَنَهَى رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم عَنْ قَتْلِ النِّسَاءِ وَالصِّبْيَانِ
rows.translation: Sunnah.com English: M. Muhsin Khan; A. H. Siddiqui
rows.says: A woman was found killed in one of the Prophet's campaigns; he disapproved of (3014) and forbade (3015) the killing of women and children.
rows.bearing: K3 Explicit for women and children (Sunni; war, rule 5). Taught in part for K3 on its own. Does not decide K1.

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1731a (Book 32, Jihad and Expeditions), Burayda; in the dataset an unnumbered item (sequence 4521) placed between 1730b and 1731c
rows.original: وَلاَ تَغُلُّوا وَلاَ تَغْدِرُوا وَلاَ تَمْثُلُوا وَلاَ تَقْتُلُوا وَلِيدًا
rows.says: When appointing a commander, the Prophet told him: fight in God's name; do not embezzle spoils, break your pledge or mutilate, and do not kill a child. Invite the enemy first to Islam, then to pay the jizya, and fight only if they refuse both.
rows.bearing: K3 Explicit for children (Sunni; war, rule 5). Taught in part for the rest of K3.

rows.reference: Sunan Abī Dāwūd 2669 (Book 15, Jihad, in-book 193), Rabāḥ ibn Rabīʿ; compare 2614 (in-book 138) and 2670 (in-book 194)
rows.original: مَا كَانَتْ هَذِهِ لِتُقَاتِلَ ... قُلْ لِخَالِدٍ لاَ يَقْتُلَنَّ امْرَأَةً وَلاَ عَسِيفًا (2669)
rows.says: Seeing people gathered round a woman killed on an expedition, the Prophet said she was not one with whom fighting should have taken place, and sent word to Khālid ibn al-Walīd not to kill a woman or a hired servant (ʿasīf) (2669). Weak reports: do not kill a decrepit old man, an infant, a child or a woman (2614); 'kill the old men (shuyūkh) of the polytheists but spare their young' (2670; the English renders sharkh as 'children').
rows.bearing: 2669: K3 Explicit for women and hired workers, with the reason (they do not fight), which gives Clear teaching of a non-combatant principle for civilians (Sunni). 2614 and 2670 are weak and do not count, so the old are protected by no counted Sunni text read here, and the one text against them (2670) also does not count.

rows.reference: Qur'an 2:190 (Sūrat al-Baqara)
rows.original: وَقَاتِلُوا فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ الَّذِينَ يُقَاتِلُونَكُمْ وَلَا تَعْتَدُوا
rows.translation: Pickthall (1930) 'begin not hostilities'; Sahih International cross-check
rows.says: Fight in the way of God against those who fight against you, but begin not hostilities (wa lā taʿtadū, also rendered 'do not transgress'); God loves not aggressors.
rows.bearing: K3: limits fighting to those who fight. Translation changes the reach: Pickthall's 'begin not hostilities' concerns who starts a war, 'do not transgress' can cover conduct in war. Al-Ṭabarī's reported readings (not killing women, children, the old) and abrogation views not checked. Implied on its own wording; Clear teaching only read with the hadith rows.
rows.strength: Implied (alone); Clear teaching with Bukhārī 3015 and Muslim 1731a

rows.reference: Qur'an 4:89 to 91 (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ)
rows.original: فَإِنِ اعْتَزَلُوكُمْ فَلَمْ يُقَاتِلُوكُمْ وَأَلْقَوْا إِلَيْكُمُ السَّلَمَ فَمَا جَعَلَ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ عَلَيْهِمْ سَبِيلًا (4:90)
rows.says: Hypocrites who turn back to enmity are to be taken and killed wherever found (4:89), except those who seek refuge with a people under covenant, or come with hearts unwilling to fight; if they hold aloof, wage no war and offer peace, God allows no way against them (4:90). Others who neither keep aloof nor offer peace nor hold their hands may be taken and killed (4:91).
rows.bearing: War context (b) for K1 and K0; 4:89 ties protection to allegiance, read by the tradition as war against hostile groups (not checked). For K3, 4:90 is Explicit that those who withdraw from fighting and offer peace may not be fought.

rows.reference: Qur'an 9:5, read with 9:4 and 9:6 (Sūrat al-Tawba); 8:61 (Sūrat al-Anfāl)
rows.original: فَاقْتُلُوا الْمُشْرِكِينَ حَيْثُ وَجَدْتُمُوهُمْ ... وَإِنْ أَحَدٌ مِنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ اسْتَجَارَكَ فَأَجِرْهُ
rows.says: When the sacred months have passed, slay the idolaters wherever you find them, take them captive, besiege them; if they repent, pray and pay the poor-due, leave their way free (9:5). Treaty partners who kept faith are excepted (9:4). If an idolater seeks protection, protect him so he may hear God's word, then convey him to his place of safety (9:6). If they incline to peace, incline to it too (8:61).
rows.bearing: War context (b); does not decide K1. For K3, 9:5 concerns whom to fight; its reported ties to treaty-breakers and abrogation debates were not checked. 9:6 is Clear teaching to protect a non-fighter who asks for safety.

rows.tier: 1 (all branches) for the verses; 2 (Sunni) for the hadith
rows.reference: Qur'an 8:67 to 69 (Sūrat al-Anfāl), with Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1763 (Book 32, Jihad and Expeditions; the captives of Badr)
rows.original: مَا كَانَ لِنَبِيٍّ أَنْ يَكُونَ لَهُ أَسْرَىٰ حَتَّىٰ يُثْخِنَ فِي الْأَرْضِ (8:67)
rows.translation: Pickthall (1930); Sunnah.com English, A. H. Siddiqui
rows.says: It is not for any prophet to have captives until he has made slaughter in the land; you desire the lure of this world (8:67); but for an earlier ordinance an awful doom had come upon you for what you took (8:68); enjoy what you have won (8:69). In Muslim 1763, after Badr Abū Bakr advised ransom and ʿUmar advised beheading the captives; the Prophet took Abū Bakr's view, then wept at the punishment shown to him for taking ransom, and the verse was revealed.
rows.bearing: A hard text for K3 on captives: within the account, God's word reproves sparing captives for ransom in that battle, after ʿUmar had advised killing them. With 47:4 (favour or ransom) and the Qurayẓa reports, the treatment of captives is disputed within the tradition (abrogation debates reported, not checked): Unclear for K3 (rule 6), in all branches because both verses are Qur'anic. War context only for K1.

rows.reference: Qur'an 47:4 (Sūrat Muḥammad)
rows.original: فَإِمَّا مَنًّا بَعْدُ وَإِمَّا فِدَاءً حَتَّىٰ تَضَعَ الْحَرْبُ أَوْزَارَهَا
rows.says: When you meet the disbelievers in battle, smite their necks until you have routed them; then make fast the bonds, and afterwards either grace or ransom, till the war lays down its burdens.
rows.bearing: War (exclusion b) for K1 and K0. For K3, the verse names only release by favour or ransom: on its face, Clear teaching that captives are not killed. Read with 8:67 to 69 and Muslim 1763 (row 45) and the Qurayẓa reports (row 48), all now read directly, the treatment of captives is disputed: Unclear for captives (rule 6).
rows.strength: Clear teaching on its face (K3, captives); disputed

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3012 (Book 56, Jihad) = Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1745a and 1745b (Book 32), al-Ṣaʿb ibn Jaththāma
rows.original: يُبَيَّتُونَ مِنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ، فَيُصَابُ مِنْ نِسَائِهِمْ وَذَرَارِيِّهِمْ قَالَ هُمْ مِنْهُمْ
rows.translation: Sunnah.com English: M. Muhsin Khan; A. H. Siddiqui
rows.says: Asked about night raids on polytheists in which some of their women and children are hit, the Prophet said: they are of them. In Muslim 1745b the questioner says 'we kill the children of the polytheists during the night raids', with the same answer.
rows.bearing: A hard text for K3. On its own wording (Bukhārī: yuṣāb, 'are hit' in a night attack) it concerns harm in raids where fighters and others cannot be told apart, not choosing to target them; al-Nawawī's and Ibn Ḥajar's reported reconciliation with Bukhārī 3015 says the same (not checked). So it does not permit deliberate killing (compare exclusion f). Muslim 1745b's wording is starker; the tradition reads both together.

rows.tier: 2 (Sunnah, treated as primary; Sunni) for Bukhārī and Muslim; Abū Dāwūd 4404 graded ṣaḥīḥ (al-Albānī, al-Arnaʾūṭ) and 2671 ḥasan (al-Albānī), counted under decision 5; Tirmidhī 1584 not checked
rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3043 (Book 56), 4121 and 4122 (Book 64); Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1768a and 1768b (Book 32); Sunan Abī Dāwūd 4404 (Book 40) and 2671 (Book 15)
rows.original: فَإِنِّي أَحْكُمُ أَنْ تُقْتَلَ الْمُقَاتِلَةُ، وَأَنْ تُسْبَى الذُّرِّيَّةُ ... لَقَدْ حَكَمْتَ فِيهِمْ بِحُكْمِ الْمَلِكِ (Bukhārī 3043)
rows.translation: Sunnah.com English: M. Muhsin Khan; A. H. Siddiqui; Ahmad Hasan
rows.says: After a siege, Banū Qurayẓa surrendered to the judgement of Saʿd ibn Muʿādh, who ruled that their fighting men be killed and their women and children taken captive; the Prophet said he had judged with the judgement of the King (God) (3043; 4121, Abū Saʿīd; 4122, ʿĀʾisha; Muslim 1768). ʿAṭiyya al-Quraẓī: captives who had grown pubic hair were killed, the rest spared (Abū Dāwūd 4404). ʿĀʾisha: no woman of Qurayẓa was killed except one, who said she had 'done a new act' (Abū Dāwūd 2671).
rows.bearing: A hard case for K3: men who had surrendered were killed under a judgement the Prophet approved, and adolescent boys were treated as fighters. The tradition is reported to read it as a judicial sentence for treaty-breaking, passed by an arbiter the tribe accepted (not checked). Whether it was an act of war or of a court is disputed, so for 'those who have surrendered' the label is Unclear (rule 6), not Contradicted. Women and children were spared, except the one woman in 2671 who is said to have done some act, which agrees with Bukhārī 3015. Ruler and war, so not K1.

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4339 (Book 64, Military Expeditions; Khālid ibn al-Walīd and Banū Jadhīma)
rows.original: اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَبْرَأُ إِلَيْكَ مِمَّا صَنَعَ خَالِدٌ
rows.says: Khālid invited Banū Jadhīma to Islam; they could not say 'aslamnā' and said 'ṣabaʾnā' (we have changed our religion). Khālid killed some and took others captive, giving each man his captive, then ordered each man to kill his captive. Ibn ʿUmar refused, and his companions with him. When told, the Prophet raised his hands and said twice: O God, I am free before You of what Khālid has done.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching for K3 that killing people who were trying to submit, and killing captives, is wrong: a counted Sunni reconciliation of the harder texts. The report states no penalty for Khālid.

rows.says: Do not fight them until they begin. If the enemy is defeated, do not kill the one who runs away, do not strike a helpless person, do not finish off the wounded. Do not inflict pain on women, even if they abuse your honour and your officers; we were ordered to desist from them although they may be unbelievers.

rows.reference: Qur'an 2:194 (Sūrat al-Baqara)
rows.original: فَمَنِ اعْتَدَىٰ عَلَيْكُمْ فَاعْتَدُوا عَلَيْهِ بِمِثْلِ مَا اعْتَدَىٰ عَلَيْكُمْ
rows.says: The forbidden month for the forbidden month, and forbidden things in retaliation. One who attacks you, attack him in like manner as he attacked you, and observe your duty to God.
rows.bearing: A proportionate response to aggression, in a war setting (rule 5). On K0 ('revenge') it allows requital in like measure only; for killing, the Qur'an routes requital through law (17:33; 2:178). Does not contradict K0 or K1.

In 4358 the Prophet orders him killed and then grants protection at ʿUthmān's request.

K1.label: Contradicted in one branch (Sunni Islam: Sunan Abī Dāwūd 4361). Twelver Shia and the Qur'an-only minority: Taught (Qur'an), with one open risk for Twelver Shia (al-Kāfī 7:259 no. 21, grade not seen). Ibadi, Zaydi and Ismaili texts not checked.
K1.reason: 1. Taught in the Qur'an for every branch (rule 7), all read directly: 5:32 forbids killing 'a human being' (nafs) with no class of victim named, a wider rule at Explicit level; 6:151, 17:33 and 25:68 forbid taking 'the life which Allah hath made sacred, save in the course of justice'; 6:140, 6:151, 17:31, 60:12 and 81:8 to 9 forbid parents to kill their children, newborn girls included (rule 9). The exceptions (a life for a life; the penalties of 5:33; the three causes of Bukhārī 6878) are penalties, context (a). Sunni Sunnah adds Explicit protection of covenanted non-Muslims (Bukhārī 3166), of a wife's alleged lover against the husband (Muslim 1498a and b: the Prophet answers 'No') and of slaves (Tirmidhī 1414, ḥasan, search). Graded protection, not permission (rule 2): Bukhārī 6915 and 111, Tirmidhī 1400, Qur'an 2:178. 2. Contradicted in the Sunni branch (rules 2, 3 and 5). Abū Dāwūd 4361, read directly and graded ṣaḥīḥ by al-Albānī and Muḥammad Muḥyī al-Dīn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd (isnād ṣaḥīḥ, Zubair ʿAlī Zaʾī), counts as Sunnah under decision 5. A blind master kills his slave woman at night, on his own authority, for repeatedly insulting the Prophet; told in the morning, the Prophet declares 'her blood is hadar' (no retaliation or blood money). Rule 2 names exactly this (a text declaring a killing wholly unpunished because of what the victim did), rule 5 names a master as a private actor, and the killing happened before any ruler knew. Counted texts that bear on it do not narrow it: Abū Dāwūd 4363 (ṣaḥīḥ) forbids killing for offending a ruler 'after Muḥammad' and records Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal's gloss that after the Prophet no one may be killed except for the three causes; Abū Dāwūd 4359 shows companions waiting for the Prophet's sign; Muslim 1498 forbids a husband's private killing. None says the blind man did wrong. No listed commentator (al-Nawawī, Ibn Ḥajar, Ibn Rajab) was checked. Abū Dāwūd 4362 (the strangled Jewish woman) is weak and does not count. 3. Path to Unclear (rule 5, last sentence; rule 6): if the project reads the Prophet's ruling after the fact, as holder of a power to kill that Aḥmad's gloss says was his alone, as making the killing judicial, or if a listed commentator is found to narrow 4361. I did not adopt that reading, because rule 2 expressly covers declarations after the fact and no counted text reads 4361 that way. Consistency: this applies rule 2 as it is applied to Numbers 35:26 to 27 for Judaism (the Mishnah reads the kinsman's killing as a private licence) and to Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2 (no narrowing text); Christianity's Numbers 35 and the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra were labelled Unclear because counted texts in those traditions narrow the hard passages, which Islam does not have for 4361 on present evidence. Phinehas (Numbers 25 with Psalm 106:30 to 31) and Yasna 31.18 and 33.2 should be labelled by the same test. 4. Twelver Shia: counted verified texts (the Qur'an) teach K1, and no verified counted Shia text contradicts it. The report quoted on al-islam.org as al-Kāfī 7:259 no. 21 (the 'most inferior' person, then the next, must kill one who reviles the Prophet, the imām last) was found only through search on a secondary page, without Arabic, narrator or grade, so it does not decide (rule 1; corpus.md: not every al-Kāfī report is sound). If it is graded reliable, K1 is also contradicted in the Twelver branch, and each main branch is then contradicted through its own texts. The al-Kāfī apostate report remains unverified. 5. Other hard texts do not decide: Qur'an 18:74 to 82 (al-Khaḍir slays a lad but says 'I did it not upon my own command', so not 'own authority'; Muslim 1812b forbids following it); 17:33 (the heir's power sits within the law of retaliation for a proven wrongful killing, context a; Unclear only if a counted text let the heir kill with no judgement, none found); Muslim 140 and Bukhārī 6902 (defence of property and privacy: limits on the exception, not contradictions); Bukhārī 6922, 4037, 3611, Muslim 1844a, Abū Dāwūd 4359 and 4462, Qur'an 5:33 and 33:61 (ruler, court or war context). 6. Qur'an-only minority: Taught (Tier 1 only; no contradicting Qur'anic text).

K0.label: Unclear in one branch (Sunni: Abū Dāwūd 4361, rule 6). Taught in the Qur'an for all branches; Twelver Shia and the Qur'an-only minority: Taught on counted verified texts, with the same open al-Kāfī risk for Twelver Shia.
K0.reason: Taught, all read directly: 5:32 (wider rule reaching every motive, Explicit). Gain: 6:151 and 17:31 (killing children because of, or fearing, poverty, Explicit), 4:29 to 30 (killing joined to consuming wealth 'through aggression and injustice', Clear teaching), and for Sunnis Bukhārī 4477 = Muslim 86a (killing one's son lest he share one's food). Anger and rivalry: 5:27 to 31 (Clear teaching: the brother slain after the rejected offering, the killer 'one of the losers'). Revenge: 17:33 ('let him not commit excess in slaying', Clear teaching), 2:178 and 42:40 (pardon preferred), and for Sunnis Muslim 1218a (the blood-revenges of the Days of Ignorance abolished, beginning with the Prophet's own kin). Hatred: 5:8 (hatred must not lead to injustice; Implied for killing). No counted text approves a killing for gain, anger, hatred or private revenge. Unclear in the Sunni branch: Abū Dāwūd 4361 approves a private killing that answers repeated insults to the Prophet. The text names no motive; whether such a killing is 'out of anger' or a religious penalty outside K0's four motives is unresolved (rule 6). If the project decides that killings presented as religious penalties fall outside K0's motives, Sunni K0 is Taught; if indignation at an insult counts as anger, it is Contradicted in one branch. This should be decided once for all traditions: the Judaism verifier treated zealot killings as outside K0's motives, while the Stoicism verifier labelled a comparable reach question Unclear. War texts (4:94, killing 'seeking the chance profits of this life') support only. If al-Kāfī 7:259 no. 21 is graded reliable, the same reach question arises for the Twelver branch.

K3.label: Unclear (all branches) for those who have surrendered and for captives; otherwise taught in part (Sunni: women, children, hired workers and non-fighters; Qur'an: those who withdraw and offer peace or ask for protection; Twelver: women, the fleeing, the helpless and the wounded; the old: no counted verified text in either branch).
K3.reason: Support read directly: Qur'an 4:90 ('if they hold aloof from you and wage not war against you and offer you peace, Allah alloweth you no way against them', Explicit), 9:6 (protect the idolater who seeks protection and convey him to safety, Clear teaching), 4:94 and 2:190, and 47:4 (captives: 'either grace or ransom', Clear teaching on its face). Sunni: Bukhārī 3015 and 3014 = Muslim 1744a and b = Abū Dāwūd 2668 (killing women and children forbidden, Explicit); Muslim 1731a ('do not kill a child'); Muslim 1812a (Ibn ʿAbbās: do not kill children); Abū Dāwūd 2669 (ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ: 'this is not one with whom fighting should have taken place'; no women or hired servants), which states the non-combatant principle (Clear teaching for civilians); Bukhārī 4339 (the Prophet disowns Khālid's killing of captives from a people trying to submit). Twelver: Nahj al-Balāgha Letter 14 (search): do not kill those who run away, strike the helpless or finish off the wounded; do not harm women 'although they may be unbelievers'. Against, all read directly: Qur'an 8:67 to 69 with Muslim 1763 (after Badr, God's word reproves taking ransom for captives, 'It is not for any prophet to have captives until he hath made slaughter in the land', ʿUmar having advised killing them); Banū Qurayẓa (Bukhārī 3043, 4121, 4122; Muslim 1768a and b; Abū Dāwūd 4404, ṣaḥīḥ, and 2671, ḥasan): men who had surrendered to Saʿd's judgement were killed, boys judged adult by pubic hair, and the Prophet called the judgement God's. Whether these are acts of war or court sentences, and how 47:4 relates to 8:67, is disputed within the tradition (abrogation debates reported, not checked), so for those who have surrendered and for captives the label is Unclear (rule 6), in all branches because 47:4 and 8:67 are Qur'anic. Bukhārī 3012 = Muslim 1745 ('they are of them') concerns women and children hit in night raids, not chosen as targets, on its own wording, so it does not contradict. objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Qur'an 18:74 to 82 is set aside as 'not own authority'. That settles a question about the reach of K1's own wording, and it does so with no project decision behind it. I read it directly (Tanzil Arabic, Pickthall, Sahih International). Al-Khaḍir is a private person, outside any court, ruler or war. He kills a lad whom Moses calls 'an innocent soul who hath slain no man' (nafsan zakiyyatan bi-ghayri nafsin, the same exception wording as 5:32). The lad was attacking no one. 18:80 gives only a fear for the future ('lest he should oppress them by rebellion and disbelief'), so K1's defence exception does not apply. The text approves the act: the servant was given 'knowledge from Our presence' (18:65), and the act was 'a mercy from their Lord ... I did it not upon my own command' (18:82). That is the exception in rule 4. K1 defines whom it binds in contrast to courts and rulers ('private persons, and anyone in charge of ...'). Rule 5 names the zealot, who also acts on what he takes to be God's will, and none of exclusions (a) to (f) covers a killing done on a divine command. The proposal treats the matching reach question in K0 (the motive in Abū Dāwūd 4361) as Unclear until a cross-tradition decision is made, and it asks that Phinehas be labelled 'by the same test'. It does not apply that test here. The Qur'an's own framing narrows the passage: the knowledge was given only to this servant, the prophet Moses could not bear the act, and the servant says it was 'not upon my own command'. For Sunnis, Muslim 1812b ('unless you could know what Khadir had known') narrows it further, so that no one may follow it. On the precedent of Christianity's Numbers 35 and the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, a hard passage that counted texts narrow is Unclear, not Taught.
objections.rule_basis: Rules 4, 5, 6 and 7. K1's binding clause and exclusions (a) to (f). Consistency with the proposal's own handling of the K0 reach question, and with the Phinehas, Numbers 35 (Christianity) and Mahāparinirvāṇa cases.
objections.proposed: Twelver Shia, and the Qur'an read alone: Unclear (rule 6), until the project decides once, for every tradition, whether K1 reaches a private killing done on a divine command that the text approves. If it decides that K1 does not reach such acts, both return to Taught. The Sunni label does not change, because 4361 decides it.

Bukhārī 6933: 'Allow me to cut off his neck'; 'Leave him.' Read with Abū Dāwūd 4359 and 4363, these show that in the Prophet's lifetime the decision was his. objections.label: K0
objections.objection: Two counted Sunni texts, read directly, make the reach question in 4361 sharper and should be in the reason. In Muslim 1680a, a man who killed another because 'he abused me and angered me' (fa-sabbanī fa-aghḍabanī) is held for retaliation, and the Prophet discourages even the lawful retaliation. In Abū Dāwūd 4363, Abū Bakr is angry with a man, and having him killed is 'not for any human after Muḥammad'. Together they are Clear teaching against killing in anger at an insult to oneself. They also show that the Sunni texts sort cases by the offence (an insult to oneself, or to the Prophet), not by the killer's motive. The strongest case for 'Contradicted in one branch' runs as follows. A plain reading at the brief's reading age takes killing someone for insulting your prophet as killing out of anger or revenge. Private religious penalties are not excluded (rule 5). And if zeal falls outside K0, every zealot killing passes the lower floor. Against that: 4361 names no motive, and the master's stated affection ('two sons like pearls', 'my companion') and his repeated warnings point to a deliberate punishment rather than anger.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: Banū Qurayẓa is labelled Unclear because 'whether these are acts of war or court sentences ... is disputed within the tradition', but that dispute is marked 'reported, not checked'. For 4361, the same proposal refused to let unchecked readings decide a label. The counted texts, read directly, approve the killings. Bukhārī 3043 and 4121: 'You have judged ... according to the King's judgment.' Bukhārī 4122: Gabriel orders the attack, and the tribe 'surrendered to the Prophet's judgment'. Bukhārī 4028: 'Qurayẓa made war (ḥārabat), so he killed their men'; the English insertion 'violating their peace treaty' is the translator's, not the Arabic. Abū Dāwūd 4404 (ṣaḥīḥ): 'I was among the captives ... those who had begun to grow hair were killed.' Abū Dāwūd 2671 (ḥasan): 'the Messenger of Allah was killing their men with the swords.' The test was status (fighting men, or puberty), not individual guilt, and that is the war category K3 addresses. Rule 5 cannot carry this into context: if a ruler's or arbiter's order in war took a killing out of K3, K3 could never be contradicted. Bukhārī 4339 (the Prophet disowns Khālid's killing of captives) is support, but under rule 2 it does not undo an approved contradiction. A lead, not deciding: Abū Dāwūd 2686 (ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ, al-Albānī; ḍaʿīf, Zubair ʿAlī Zaʾī) says only that the Prophet 'intended to kill your father' and answered 'Fire' to 'who will look after my children?'. That the father was a captive is not in the text read, so it does not decide.

'He brought those of the People of the Scripture who supported them down from their strongholds ... Some ye slew, and ye made captive some.' K1.reason: 1. Qur'an (all branches). Explicit support, read directly: 5:32 (a wider rule: nafs, with no class of victim named), 6:151, 17:33 and 25:68 ('save in the course of justice'), and 6:140, 17:31, 60:12 and 81:8 to 9 for children from birth (rule 9). The exceptions are penalties framed as matters of judging (5:44 to 48; 2:178), so they are context (a). 4:89 to 91 is war on its own words (fighting, 'hold their hands', 'offer you peace'). One Tier 1 hard text is unresolved: 18:74 to 82. A private person outside any court, ruler or war kills a lad who 'hath slain no man', and the text approves it (rule 4). Whether K1's 'own authority' reaches an act done on a divine command that the text approves is a question about K1's wording. The Qur'an itself narrows the passage ('knowledge from Our presence'; 'not upon my own command'; Moses could not bear it). On the precedent of Christianity's Numbers 35 and the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, that makes it Unclear (rule 6) until the project decides the question once for every tradition. 2. Sunni: Contradicted in one branch. Abū Dāwūd 4361 was read directly. Grades: ṣaḥīḥ (al-Albānī; Muḥammad Muḥyī al-Dīn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd) and isnād ṣaḥīḥ (Zubair ʿAlī Zaʾī). A blind master kills his umm walad at night, on his own authority, for repeatedly insulting the Prophet. Next morning the Prophet declares 'her blood is hadar' (no retaliation and no blood money; the English 'no retaliation is payable' understates the Arabic). He imposes no expiation and states no blame. Rule 2 names exactly this case, and rule 5 names a master as a private actor. Counted Sunni texts on the ruler's role (Bukhārī 6926, 2617, 4905 and 6933; Abū Dāwūd 4359, and 4363 with Aḥmad's gloss) show companions asking the Prophet's leave and being refused. None concerns a killing done without asking, and none says the blind man did wrong, so they do not narrow 4361. Two more Sunni texts have an unresolved reach on their own words (Bukhārī 3611; Abū Dāwūd 4462). They would keep the branch at Unclear even if 4361 were narrowed. Path to Unclear: a listed commentator (al-Nawawī, Ibn Ḥajar, Ibn Rajab; none checked) reading 4361 as a judicial act of the Prophet that bars private killing. Graded protection, not permission: Bukhārī 6915; Tirmidhī 1400; Qur'an 2:178. Further Sunni support: Bukhārī 3166, Muslim 1498a and b, and Tirmidhī 1414 (search only). 3. Twelver Shia: no verified counted Shia text contradicts K1, so the label follows the Qur'an. It is Unclear on 18:74 to 82, and Taught if the project rules divine commands outside K1. If either al-Kāfī report is confirmed and graded reliable, K1 is Contradicted in the Twelver branch as well. 4. Other hard texts are context or limits: 5:33 and 33:61 (ruler); Bukhārī 4037, 6922 and 1846 (ruler or war); Muslim 140 and Bukhārī 6902 (limits on the defence exception); Muslim 1812b (forbids following al-Khaḍir). Abū Dāwūd 4360 and 4362 are weak and are not counted.

K0.label: Unclear in one branch (Sunni: Abū Dāwūd 4361, motive not named; this is a question about K0's reach, to be decided once for every tradition). Twelver Shia, and the Qur'an read alone: Taught, with the same open al-Kāfī risk for Twelver Shia. Ibadi, Zaydi and Ismaili texts not checked.
K0.reason: Qur'an (all branches), read directly. 5:32 is a wider rule that reaches every motive (Explicit). Gain: 6:151 and 17:31 (Explicit); 4:29 to 30, 'through aggression and injustice' (Clear teaching). Anger and rivalry: 5:27 to 31 (Clear teaching). Revenge: 17:33 ('let him not commit excess in slaying'), 2:178 ('he who transgresseth after this'), and 5:45 and 42:40, where pardon is preferred. Al-Khaḍir's stated motive (18:80: to prevent future harm to the parents) is none of K0's four, so 18:74 to 82 does not bear on K0. Sunni support: Bukhārī 4477 = Muslim 86a (killing for gain); Muslim 1218a (blood-revenges of the Days of Ignorance abolished); Muslim 1680a (a man who killed one who 'abused me and angered me' is held for retaliation, and the Prophet discourages retaliation: 'if he kills him, he is like him'); and Abū Dāwūd 4363 (killing a man who angered the caliph is 'not for any human after Muḥammad'). Sunni label: Unclear (rule 6). Abū Dāwūd 4361 declares hadar a private killing that answers insults to the Prophet, but names no motive. The counted Sunni texts condemn killing in anger at an insult to oneself and clear a killing that answers insults to the Prophet. They sort cases by the offence, not by the motive. A plain reading favours 'reaches', which would give Contradicted in one branch. The master's stated affection and his repeated warnings favour a deliberate punishment rather than anger, which would give Taught. Twelver Shia: Taught on the Qur'an. If al-Kāfī 7:259 no. 21 is confirmed and graded reliable, the same question about K0's reach arises there.

K3.label: Sunni: Contradicted in one branch for those who have surrendered and for captives taken at surrender (Banū Qurayẓa); Unclear for refuge-seekers named individually for death (Ibn Khaṭal); Taught for women, children, hired workers and, by the reason Abū Dāwūd 2669 gives, all who do not fight, the old included. All branches (Qur'an): taught in part (4:90, 9:6, 47:4); Unclear for captives and the surrendered (8:67 to 69; 33:26). Twelver Shia: taught in part (women, those who flee, the helpless and the wounded); children and the old: no counted verified Twelver text; captives and the surrendered: Unclear (Qur'an).
K3.reason: All branches, from the Qur'an read directly. Support: 4:90 (those who 'hold aloof ... and offer you peace': 'Allah alloweth you no way against them', Explicit); 9:6 (protect the one who seeks protection, Clear teaching); 47:4 (captives: 'either grace or ransom', Clear teaching on its face); 2:190 (Implied on its own). Hard texts: 8:67 to 69 (no captives 'until he hath made slaughter in the land'; on its own words it reproves taking captives for gain, and 8:69 makes the spoils lawful, so it does not itself approve killing captives); and 33:26 ('Some ye slew, and ye made captive some', of those brought down from their strongholds, presented as God's favour; whether they were killed after surrender is not stated). So captives and the surrendered are Unclear in all branches on the Qur'an's own words (rule 6). Sunni, read directly: Bukhārī 3043, 4121, 4122 and 4028, Muslim 1768, and Abū Dāwūd 4404 (ṣaḥīḥ) and 2671 (ḥasan). They approve, as 'the King's judgment', the killing of men who had surrendered and of captive boys judged adult by pubic hair. The test was status, not individual guilt. The 'judicial sentence for treason' reading is unchecked, and on the standard used for 4361 it does not decide. So the label is Contradicted in one branch for this class. It becomes Unclear only if a listed commentator reads the event as a judicial sentence and the project decides that K3 does not reach such sentences. Bukhārī 4339 (the Prophet disowns Khālid's killing of captives) supports K3 but does not undo the contradiction (rule 2). Ibn Khaṭal (Bukhārī 1846 = 3044) was a named individual killed on order at the conquest, with no reason given in the text, so whether it was a penalty or an act of war is unresolved: Unclear. Taught for women and children (Bukhārī 3014 and 3015; Muslim 1744; Muslim 1731a; Muslim 1812a) and for hired workers. By 2669's stated reason ('this was not one to fight'), the protection reaches all who do not fight, the old included (Clear teaching, wider principle; rule 7). The weak Abū Dāwūd 2614 and 2670 do not count. Night raids (Bukhārī 3012; Muslim 1745) do not contradict: the Arabic of 1745b is nuṣību ('we hit'), not 'we kill', and Abū Dāwūd 2672 (ṣaḥīḥ) records al-Zuhrī: 'Thereafter the Messenger of Allah prohibited to kill women and children'. Twelver Shia: Nahj al-Balāgha Letter 14 (search only) protects women 'although they may be unbelievers', those who flee, the helpless and the wounded. The al-Kāfī war report naming the old, children and women is unverified. K3 is a record wording, so no floor depends on it.

challenge.consistency_notes: 1. Abū Dāwūd 4361 is treated like Numbers 35:26 to 27 in Judaism and Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2 in Stoicism. A counted text declares a private killing wholly unpunished, and no counted narrowing was found, so the result is Contradicted (in one branch here, because only Sunnis accept Abū Dāwūd). It is not treated like Christianity's Numbers 35 or the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
